title: Stack and Heap
body:
Local variables are allocated inside the stack.

***The Heap***
a.k.a runtime heap

---

Two regions of [[Memory]] with completely different rules, and knowing which one a value is in
answers most questions about why a program broke.

| | Stack | Heap |
|---|---|---|
| Holds | locals, parameters, return addresses | whatever you `new` |
| Allocated by | entering a block | you, explicitly |
| Freed by | leaving the block | you, explicitly |
| Size decided | compile time | run time |
| Cost | a register moves, effectively free | a real search for a free chunk |
| Failure mode | stack overflow | memory leak |

```c++
void f() {
	int a = 5;              // stack, gone at the closing brace
	int *p = new int(5);    // p is on the stack, *p is on the heap
	delete p;               // or *p stays allocated forever
}
```

The stack grows and shrinks with the call chain. Every [[Function]] call pushes a frame
holding its parameters, its locals, and where to return to; the return pops it. That is why
locals cannot be forgotten about and why unbounded [[Recursion]] blows the stack: the frames
pile up and nothing pops them. [[Subroutines]] in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] shows the actual
push and pop instructions doing this.

The heap has no such structure. Nothing pops it for you, which is what
[[Variable Lifetime|lifetime]] means for dynamic storage and why [[new And delete]] insists on
the matching `delete`.

The rule that follows: **never return a pointer to a local.** The stack frame is reclaimed at
the return, so the caller is holding an address to memory that is about to be reused. Return
heap memory (and say who has to delete it) or return by value.
